title: His will as yours (Avot 2:4)
hookLine: make God's will your will, so God makes your will His
last: TWO HANDS, EACH KEEPING THE OTHER STEADY.

lines: FROM HAVE TO, TO WANT TO.
cards: A kid cleans his room because he's told to. Years later, grown up, he cleans it because he actually likes a clean room. Same broom, same floor.
But something changed inside: the rule stopped being someone else's and became his. That shift, from have to, to want to, is what today's saying is about.
It's a bold line, and it talks about God's will and yours as if they could become the same thing.

teach.b: Rabban Gamaliel, son of Rabbi Judah, says this. Do His will as if it were your will, so that He will do your will as if it were His.
Set aside your will before His will, so that He will set aside the will of others before yours. The Hebrew for will is ratzon: what you want, what pleases you, your desire.

teach.h: A SAYING BUILT LIKE A MIRROR.
teach.b: The saying is built like a mirror, your will and God's reflected back and forth. Commentators read it more than one way.
Some take it practically: spend on doing good as gladly as you spend on what you want for yourself, and good things will come back to you. Others hear something inward.
At first a commandment feels like someone else's rule.

teach.h: FROM HAVE TO, TO WANT TO.
teach.b: Over years of doing it, you can come to want it, the way the kid comes to want the clean room. Then what God wants and what you want aren't two different things anymore. The second half is harder.
Sometimes what you want and what's good really do pull apart, and the saying asks you to let the good win. It doesn't promise you'll always get your way.
It speaks of God setting aside the will of others, the pressure and plans of people around you, on your behalf.
So the carry is simple: want what's good.

And it closes a week of sayings: someone else's share was in the pile, silence, truth, justice and peace, it will be well with you, Malachi's book, two hands, each keeping the other steady, and today, his will as yours.

how: Some Jewish teachers describe growth in observance as moving from doing a commandment because it is commanded to doing it with love, and this saying is studied as a picture of that change.

o: a commandment you keep because you must
will: what you want, what pleases you
the reward God gives for a good deed

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: so He does your will as His
so He sets aside the will of others
spend on good as gladly as on yourself

s: the saying promises you'll always get your way
it asks you to set your will aside, and speaks of God setting aside the pressure of others.
ratzon means will, desire, what pleases you
the saying mirrors God's ratzon and yours.
commentators read this saying only one way
some read it practically, about spending on good; others inwardly, about coming to want it.

games.q: you do a good thing every week, but only because you have to. what does Rabban Gamaliel's saying hope for?
o: that you stop, since your heart isn't in it.
that over time you come to want it.
that you keep doing it and never mind why.
games.why: do His will as if it were your will. some teachers read it as the slow change from have to, to want to.

practice: Let one strong want come up, a thing, a result, someone's approval, and look at it honestly without pushing it away. Is there a good version inside it?
Wanting money might hide wanting to care for someone; wanting to win might hide wanting to be seen. Let the wish lean toward that good thing, and if you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Ratzon. Will, what you want: the word behind Rabban Gamaliel's mirror, do God's will as if it were your own.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: do His will as your will.

carryVoice: Your line: want what's good. Have to can grow into want to. See you tomorrow.
